display_title: A well written and well explained paper.

content.title: A well written and well explained paper.
content.review:
The authors have clearly explained the paper and provided justifications about what problem they are solving. The paper proposes a Mem2Mem (memory-to-memory mechanism) for the task of abstractive document summarization. 

Pros:
* The work achieves comparable to better results even when compared with larger networks like GPT-2. 
* Ablation studies justifies the use of regularization methods over baseline HRED models. 

Cons: 

* While the idea is well explained, the novelty of the paper is hard to justify. The work with memory networks and the design has been used in the past and this work seems like an extension of several works in the past. (Lin et al., Kim et al. ). Also, the comparison with Kim et al. MMN would be easier to understand the differences. Or fair differences needs to be pointed out. 

* The memory architecture seems like an engineering work over memory read/write mechanism for general seq2seq models proposed by Benmalek et al. It is sure an improvement over it, but lacks thinking from new angle. Would be interesting to understand the differences from the authors point of view. 

* "The Mem2Mem’s memory compression can be generalized to other domains that require text generation guided by content selection". No discussions has been done regarding this by the authors and the claims need to be justified with some proofs/experiments. It is unclear as of now how that is possible.
content.confidence: 3: The reviewer is fairly confident that the evaluation is correct

content.title: Fundamental differences with related works
content.comment:
We appreciate your effort in reviewing our paper. We will address each comment in the following bullet points.

* It is true that we were inspired by other works you’ve mentioned. However, our memory regularization is a novel application of Lin’s work to memory compression for long text generation. In addition, Mem2Mem has the following fundamental differences with MMN by Kim et al. First, Unlike MMN, Mem2Mem compresses the hierarchical representation of the document into a sparse set of sentence representations. It is shown in our analysis that the memory compression mechanism is able to prioritize salient sentences amongst a large set of input sentences [Table3]. Second, MMN’s memory representations remain static throughout the decoding process while Mem2Mem dynamically updates its memory. The dynamic update of memory is effective in keeping track of what's been attended so far [Benmalek et al.], which is crucial for long text generation. Finally, MMN was evaluated on the reddit-TIFU dataset, whose input document length is much shorter than that of PubMed and arXiv (432.6 (Tiffu-Long) vs 3224.4 (PubMed) or 6913.8 (arXiv)) datasets. We will highlight these differences in the next version.
* As stated above, our memory write mechanism is indeed inspired by Benmalek et al. However, we found a way to make this work for long text summarization in a more efficient way. The computational complexity of the scratchpad mechanism is O(L x N) where L is the length of the input document and N is that of the corresponding summary. In our Mem2Mem, we reduce L to M, the number of memory heads where M << L. We also adapted the scratchpad attention mechanism for hierarchical RNNs which was not done before. We appreciate you raised this point and will highlight this improvement in the next version.
* Although we haven’t verified the potential of memory compression in other tasks, it is not the primary focus of this work. That is why we mentioned it in Conclusion as future work. Throughout the paper, our main goal was to demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed memory architectures and regularizations on long text summarization. In the next version, we will make this point clear and remove any ambiguities.

content.title: Mem2Mem Review
content.review:
The paper proposed an abstractive summarization approach by leveraging external memory modules. The idea is to have a hybrid extractive and abstractive summarization approach without the supervision on the binary ground truth labels for the extractive step.

The method has a limited novelty with respect to the architecture of the approach. Memory networks have been already used in summarization (kim et al) and Benmalek et al previously proposed the application of external memories equipped with encoder/decoder methods for language generation and more importantly the model performance is not comparable with the state-of-the-art approaches such as PEGASUS ICML 2020  on the same datasets. So, considering that the architecture is not novel and having an implicit hybrid extractive and abstractive summarization with proposed architecture  cannot necessarily outperform the existing methods, I think the contribution of the paper does not seem sufficient.

They proposed an abstractive summarization approach by leveraging external memory modules. The idea is to have a hybrid extractive and abstractive summarization approach without the supervision on the binary ground truth labels for the extractive step.

display_title: PEGASUS is a pretrained model that uses much more data and many more parameters

content.title: PEGASUS is a pretrained model that uses much more data and many more parameters
content.comment:
We appreciate your insightful comments. We will address specific key points in the following.

-  Our memory write mechanism is indeed inspired by Benmalek et al. However, we found a way to make this work for long text summarization. The scratchpad attention mechanism keeps in memory L x N gradients for input size of L and a summary of N. We reduce L to M where M << L. We also adapted the scratchpad attention mechanism for hierarchical RNNs which was not done before.
- PEGASUS is a pretrained model that uses much more data and many more parameters. New research shows however that it is possible to come close to fine-tuned pretrained models with "from scratch" training. We will adapt our paper and cite PEGASUS.
- Our approach is novel because we use a combination of elements in a novel way (compression mechanism + external memory + hierarchy + memory regularization + memory write). This however is not our main story. The fact that you stress this particular point shows that we have not done enough to highlight the benefits of our method. We will add more analysis in the next version.

display_title: Mem2Mem vs vanilla attention mechanism vs other summarization frameworks?

content.title: Mem2Mem vs vanilla attention mechanism vs other summarization frameworks?
content.review:
The paper proposes memory-to-memory mechanism (Mem2Mem) for long-form summarization, which extends the encoder-decoder framework with encoder/decoder memory banks dynamically updated during text generation. Results show that a hierarchical RNN-based model with Mem2Mem is competitive with a Transformer-based summarization model in three different datasets.

Some questions and comments:

1. It is mentioned in the paper that one disadvantage of current models is the use of multi-step training or reinforcement learning. Why and in what aspect are these at a disadvantage? Is there a performance gap between these methods and the proposed one? It is hard to answer this question because there is no comparison shown in the paper regarding this statement.
2. The paper emphasizes that the whole process of Mem2Mem can essentially be seen as extraction followed by generation. However, can't the same thing be said about attention mechanism in a hierarchical architecture, i.e. the attention weights can be seen as the probability of selecting the sentence. Isn't it more appropriate to say (in both memory and attention architectures) that the process is more ike a (soft-)clustering of the sentences into different topics?
3. One advantage of the method mentioned in the paper is that it removes the necessity of using a pre-extractive stage, especially for longer documents. There are multiple frameworks that have been proposed before that replaces the extractive-then-abstractive summarization framework. For example, [1] has investigated on some of these frameworks, and in fact they showed results on PubMed and arXiv as well, which is significantly better than what is shown in this paper. The paper would be more convincing if it had shown these comparisons as well.
4. Table 3 shows comparisons between unsupervised extractive methods and an extractive version of the proposed model using memory weights. In connection to question #2, how would using the attention weights to extract sentences perform compared to the proposed model?
5. The paper provides human evaluation results using a subset of the arXiv dataset. They hired Amazon Mechanical Turk workers to read and annotate 20 random article-summary pairs. Based on the information given, there are a couple of issues. It is not ensured that the annotators are knowledgable enough to annotate research papers, especially since these papers tend to be very technical for a lay person to read easily. How are "important points" judged by the annotators when judging informativeness? How much time was given to read one very long paper and to judge its corresponding summary?

[1] https://arxiv.org/pdf/2006.10213.pdf
content.confidence: 4: The reviewer is confident but not absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct

display_title: Memory holds a smaller selected subset of the input text so attention to memory content is less costly.

content.title: Memory holds a smaller selected subset of the input text so attention to memory content is less costly.
content.comment:
Thank you for taking the time to read our paper and to post a very thoughtful review. We will address each comment in the following bullet points.

1. The main disadvantage of multi-step training is that you would most likely need labels for your extraction step. Further, connecting a "hard attention mechanism" (akin to the extraction step) to a language model often requires reinforcement learning policy gradient methods, which are known to be high variance. We require neither labels nor gradient estimation.
2. The probability mass of the compression mechanism is concentrated on one sentence. We see this type of sparsity of the memory content in figure 2a. Each sentence representation from the memory module is then used to produce each sentence in the summary. If the memory contained the entirety of the sentences in the article, the comparison with clustering would be justified. However, the memory only holds 2-4% of the input sentences. The rest of the input sentences have zero-probability mass.
3. Thank you for suggesting this paper! It does indeed address similar issues. Our paper has been public on openreview since last year. Since progress in the field is very fast, we will need to adapt to new research. We will cite this paper.
4. Great question. We will add results from the pure attention mechanism. As mentioned before, one draw back of attending directly to sentences is that the probability mass is highly distributed.
5. Another great question. We were under pressure from past conference reviews to add human evaluations even if Amazon Mechanical Turk workers would not necessary be able to assess scientific articles. Since we had spent our budget on human evaluations, we have added the results. To make the evaluation more manageable for Amazon Mechanical Turk workers, we had to truncate the article. We will add details about the process in the appendix.

content.title: The comparsion with SOTA architectures
content.comment:
Dear reviewers,
We appreciate your time in reviewing the paper and insightful feedback.
Some comments raised the issue around the comparison with SOTA works on the same dataset. The following table compares our model with the latest SOTA architectures. The evaluation metrics are Rouge-1/2/L.

|         Model        | Type | # of param |       PubMed      |       ArXiv       |
|:--------------------:|:----:|:----------:|:-----------------:|:-----------------:|
| Ptr-Gen-Seq2Seq [1]  |   A  |      -     | 35.86/10.22/29.69 | 32.06/9.04/25.16  |
| Discourse-aware  [1] |   A  |    14.3M   | 38.93/15.37/35.21 | 35.80/11.05/31.80 |
| Mem2Mem (ours)       |   A  |    14.7M   | 42.06/16.56/38.11 | 41.81/14.99/37.24 |
| TLM [2]              |   A  |    234M    | 37.06/11.69/34.27 | 39.65/12.15/35.76 |
| TLM [2]              |   H  |    234M    | 42.13/16.27/39.21 | 41.62/14.69/38.03 |
| Trunc [3]            |   A  |    223M    | 39.80/15.50/24.30 | 32.90/11.30/20.70 |
| PEGASUS_base [4]     |   A  |    223M    | 39.98/15.15/25.23 | 34.81/10.16/22.50 |
| PEGASUS_large [4]    |   A  |    568M    | 45.49/19.90/27.69 | 44.70/17.27/25.80 |
| SEAL [3]             |   A  |    223M    | 46.50/20.10/42.20 | 44.30/18.00/39.30 |

([1] Cohan et al. (2018), [2] Subramanian et al. (2019), [3] Zhang et al. (2020), [4] Zhao et al. (2020))

We believe it is worthy of note that Mem2Mem surpasses or shows comparable results to the most Transformer-based models with an order of magnitude less parameters (TLM, Trunc, PEGASUS_base). The only two models that significantly outperform Mem2Mem are PEGASUS_large [4] and SEAL [3]. However, PEGASUS_large is pre-trained on large text corpora such as C4 and HugeNews, and has over x38 larger parameters. Besides, SEAL benefits from not truncating input text, and has x12 larger parameters. Given the limited capacity of Mem2Mem, we think it shows promising results.

Regarding the comments about architectural novelty, although Mem2Mem's architecture is not pushing the boundary of SOTA, it successfully integrates different elements into a single end-to-end framework for long text summarization. We also proposed novel regularization methods that enable such integration. We wonder if reviewers would take these points into further consideration to adjust their scores. If the aforementioned points are not sufficient for reconsideration, we will withdraw and improve our work based on reviewer's comments.
